questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=3x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 5$ and $-3\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-3}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,3u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,-3\le v\le 3}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\cdot ⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-2v)\cdot (-3)+(-v)\cdot (2)+2u\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+6v-2v+2u \\  & =-7u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-7u+4v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(-7u+4v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
For a surface $S$ given by $y=-{x}^{2}z$ for $(x,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(\,xz+Q+\,{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

*Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive  $j$-component.*
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y=-{x}^{2}z,$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,z)=⟨x,\,-{x}^{2}z,z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,-2xz,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨0,\,-{x}^{2},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2xz & 0 \\ 0 & -{x}^{2} & 1\end{aligned}|=⟨-2xz,\,-1,\,-{x}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

However, notice that the $j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction:

$$
{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{x}^{′}=-{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′}=⟨2xz,\,1,\,{x}^{2}⟩
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,z))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,R\,⟩\cdot ⟨2xz,\,1,\,{x}^{2}⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2P\,xz+Q+R\,{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy)$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-x\le y\le 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy))=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy))=\frac{x}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $F$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy)} \\  & =⟨{{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-({cos}^{2}⁡(xy))\cdot (\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)})-({cos}^{2}⁡(xy))\cdot (\frac{x}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)})+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-x+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-x}^{0}(-y-x+1)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-xy+y]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-{x}^{2}+x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x)\,dx \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{xy(2x+y)}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 2-(-y)\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7x}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨x+y,\,y-x,\,z⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $F$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨x+y,\,y-x,\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨x+y,\,y-x,\,z⟩{|}_{z=1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y-x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x+y,\,y-x,\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot (2x)-(y-x)\cdot (2y)+1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2{x}^{2}-2xy-2{y}^{2}+2xy+1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[y-{x}^{2}y-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=-1}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[(1-{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3})-(-1+{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3})]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2-2{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2x-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(2-\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3})-(-2+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z={e}^{x-y}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le x.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}={e}^{x-y} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}=-{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩{|}_{z={e}^{x-y}} \\  & =⟨{e}^{-(x-y)},\,xy{e}^{-(x-y)},\,{e}^{x-y}⟩ \\  & =⟨{{{e}^{y-x}}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{xy{e}^{y-x}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{e}^{x-y}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-{e}^{y-x}\cdot {e}^{x-y}-(xy{e}^{y-x})\cdot (-{e}^{x-y})+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+xy+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}(-1+xy+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-y+\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}-{e}^{x-y}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}-1+{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}-x+{e}^{x}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{8}-1+e)-1 \\  & =-\frac{19}{8}+e\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067725/assets/3761b12939f74f1e7f4d01ca83ea2884c1296672e22128064b109f7c42bb4df6.png)

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: -3u+2v \right\rangle
$$

over the domain 

$$
D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 2, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z+2y,\,3y+z,\,x-z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=-3u+2v} \\  & =⟨(-3u+2v)+2v,\,3v+(-3u+2v),\,u-(-3u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-3u+4v,\,-3u+5v,\,4u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(-3u+4v)\cdot (3)+(-3u+5v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+12v+6u-10v+4u-2v \\  & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+2y,\,3y+z,\,x-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}u\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is ${\color{blue}u}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D 
\Bigg( 
\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} 
+ Q 
- \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z}
\Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

*Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive  $\mathbf j$-component.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y = h(x,z),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,z) = \left\langle x, \: h(x,z),\: z \right\rangle.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨0,\frac{∂h}{∂z},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & \frac{∂h}{∂x} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{∂h}{∂z} & 1\end{aligned}|=⟨\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,-1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂z}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

However, notice that the $\mathbf j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction:

$$
\mathbf{r}'_z \times \mathbf{r}'_x = - \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_z =   \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}, \: 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right \rangle
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,z))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂h}{∂x},\,1,\,-\frac{∂h}{∂z}⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}+Q-R\frac{∂h}{∂z})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x, y, z) = \left\langle -y, \: x, \: z+2 \right\rangle,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x^2+y^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2x)-(x)\cdot (2y)+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-2xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+2y]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7x}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
